# Normalized hinge stress when the continuous fibers are intervals

This is a limited-dimensional normalization theorem for the potential in
`candidate de8d1a3251731edd`. It does not
establish the OC budget, and it does not settle normalization when
`d>=2`.

Let `P subset Z^n` be finite and nonempty, and let the positive fibers be
intervals `K_z=[l_z,r_z]`, `l_z<r_z`. Fix a feasible cap count `N` and
budget `0<tau<1`. At EVERY local minimum of the continuously normalized
full-cover hinge potential, the joint cap/section/contact equations
(15)--(19) of that note have a solution with objective multiplier
`alpha_0=1`.

No strict feasibility assumption is necessary. The new mechanism is a
local error bound for finitely many piecewise-affine constraints; it is
not a generic constraint qualification.

## 1. The reduced finite-dimensional constraints are piecewise affine

When `d=1`, a unit continuous normal is `u_i=+1` or `u_i=-1`. These signs
are constant in a neighborhood of any candidate minimum. The local
variables are the integer coefficients and thresholds `(a_i,b_i)`.
Write `t_iz=b_i-a_i dot z`.

For `u_i=+1`, the cap length in fiber `z` is

`[r_z-max(l_z,t_iz)]_+`.

For `u_i=-1`, it is

`[min(r_z,-t_iz)-l_z]_+`.

These are continuous piecewise-affine functions of the parameters.
Their finite sums give the exact cap-mass constraints.

The whole-fiber cover margin

`F_z=min_(x in [l_z,r_z]) max_i(u_i x-t_iz)`

is also continuous piecewise affine. One explicit description suffices
to verify this without a parametric-optimization regularity assumption.
For positive-sign caps let `p_z=min_(u_i=+1) t_iz`; for negative-sign caps
let `q_z=max_(u_i=-1)(-t_iz)`. When both signs occur,

`max_i(u_i x-t_iz)=max(x-p_z,q_z-x)`.

Its minimum on the interval is attained at the projection of
`(p_z+q_z)/2` onto `[l_z,r_z]`; substituting the three possible pieces
gives a continuous piecewise-affine expression. With just one sign the
minimum is at the appropriate interval endpoint and is affine after
the finite minimum/maximum defining its threshold. Thus the exact
feasible constraints are

`g_i=mu(H_i)-tau M<=0`, `g_z=-F_z<=0`,

a finite family of continuous piecewise-affine functions on a Euclidean
parameter space. They admit a common finite partition into closed
polyhedra on each of which every function is affine.

## 2. A self-contained local error bound

Let `g_1,...,g_k` be any finite family of continuous piecewise-affine
functions, and let `X={p:g_j(p)<=0 for all j}`. At each `p_* in X`
there are a neighborhood and a finite `C` such that

`dist(p,X)<=C max_j (g_j(p))_+`.                               (1)

Here is the needed finite-polyhedron argument. For a nonempty polyhedron
`Y={p:A p<=b}`, let `y` be the Euclidean projection of `p` onto `Y`,
and put `v=p-y`. Its projection inequality says that `v` lies in the
cone generated by the normals of constraints active at `y`; this is
the elementary separating-hyperplane description of the normal cone
of an intersection of finitely many halfspaces. Choose a representation

`v=sum_(j in J) lambda_j A_j`, `lambda_j>=0`,

with the active row vectors in `J` linearly independent. Such a choice
is possible by eliminating a linear dependence from any nonnegative
representation until its support is independent. The least singular
value of this independent row family gives

`sum_(j in J) lambda_j <= C_J |v|`

for a finite constant `C_J` depending only on that family. Since every
row is active at `y`,

`|v|^2=sum_J lambda_j(A_j p-b_j)
        <=C_J |v| max_j(A_j p-b_j)_+`.

Taking the maximum over the finitely many independent row families
proves a finite linear-inequality error bound. Zero distance needs no
division. The normal-cone statement used here follows directly by
separating `v` from the finitely generated normal cone: a separating
direction would keep every active inequality feasible to first order,
all inactive inequalities remain feasible for a sufficiently small
step, and its positive pairing with `v` contradicts the projection
inequality.

Now use a common polyhedral partition for the `g_j`. In a sufficiently
small neighborhood of `p_*`, only cells whose closures contain `p_*`
occur, because there are finitely many closed cells. On each such cell
`R`, the set `X intersect R` is a nonempty polyhedron (it contains
`p_*`). Apply the preceding bound to its affine `g_j` inequalities and
the cell's own inequalities. For `p in R`, violations of the cell
inequalities are zero, leaving exactly the right side of (1).
The maximum of the finitely many constants proves (1).

## 3. Exact penalty and a normalized stationarity equation

The hinge objective `Psi` is continuously differentiable and locally
Lipschitz in these parameters: every interval cap boundary has zero
length measure, so its gradient is the actual cap-mass/first-moment
gradient from (9) of the main note.

At a constrained local minimum `p_*`, let `L` be a local Lipschitz
constant. The nearest feasible point supplied by (1) stays in the
local-minimum neighborhood when `p` is sufficiently near `p_*`.
Consequently

`Psi(p)>=Psi(p_*)-LC max_j(g_j(p))_+`.

Thus `p_*` is an unconstrained local minimum of the exact penalty

`Psi(p)+LC sum_j(g_j(p))_+`.

Its finite-dimensional generalized gradient condition gives

`0 in grad Psi(p_*) + sum_j t_j partial g_j(p_*)`,
`0<=t_j<=LC`, with `t_j=0` for inactive constraints.             (2)

For clarity, this normalized condition follows by separating zero from
the compact convex generalized gradient of the penalty if it did not
contain zero; the separating direction would strictly decrease the
locally Lipschitz penalty. The sum and positive-part upper-gradient
rules yield the displayed representation. The coefficient of the
objective is exactly one because the error bound produced an exact
penalty before separation. No Slater argument is used.

Cap-mass gradients in (2) have precisely the consistent interval-section
form `(P_i^s,-S_i)`: at interior section points the density is one, at
an endpoint it lies in `[0,1]`, and an absent section contributes zero.
The same density is used in both entries.

## 4. Lifting the coverage gradients to actual contacts

The generalized gradients of an active `-F_z` are convex combinations
of its finite affine pieces. Each limiting active piece comes from a
primal-dual minimax certificate for the interval. Its cap weights are
either one cap (an endpoint optimum) or an equally weighted positive/
negative pair (an interior optimum); limits and ties give convex
combinations of these weights.

At the limiting configuration `F_z=0`, each of these weights is dual
optimal in (6) of the main note. Indeed the coefficients converge and
the interval is fixed and compact. A convex combination of dual-optimal
weights is again dual optimal, because the dual objective is concave
and never exceeds the primal value zero. Thus the combined coverage
gradient in (2) has one weight vector `lambda_z in Delta_N` that is
still dual optimal.

Choose ANY primal minimizer `x_z` of the maximum on the interval. A
primal and a dual optimum are a saddle pair: every cap margin at
`x_z` is nonpositive, its `lambda_z` average is zero, and
`-sum_i lambda_zi u_i in N_Kz(x_z)`. Every positively weighted margin
therefore vanishes. This produces the same actual mixed-integer
contact required in (8).

The unrestricted `(a_i,b_i)` equations in (2) now give exactly

`c_i+r_i S_i=sum_z eta_z lambda_zi`,
`P_i+r_i P_i^s=sum_z eta_z lambda_zi z`.

There are no tangent variations of a one-dimensional unit normal:
the sphere is `{+1,-1}`. Its scalar normal multiplier is free. Using
the common cap-contact equality and the actual section equation
`L_i=0` in the two displayed identities gives

`m_i+r_i m_i^s=sum_z eta_z lambda_zi x_z+Psi_i u_i`.

For example, multiply this last claimed identity by `u_i=+1` or `-1`;
its difference reduces exactly to the already proved offset and base
equations plus `integral_H L_i=Psi_i`. Hence no additional rotation
assumption is hidden in the lift. All the main note's equations hold
with `alpha_0=1`, as asserted. QED.

## 5. Limitation

When `d>=2`, cap masses and support functions are not generally
piecewise affine in their continuous-normal directions, and the local
error bound (1) has not been proved. This argument therefore does not
settle whether strict feasibility alone guarantees a normal joint
hinge stress in arbitrary dimension.
